newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ousted HK immigration chief denies corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ousted HK immigration chief denies corruption.

text.p: Hong Kong's former immigration chief said on Friday he was forced out of his job last year, contradicting the government's version of his sudden departure.

Laurence Leung, testifying under oath to a Legislative Council panel of inquiry, also said he had been investigated -- and cleared -- by Hong Kong's powerful anti-graft watchdog, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Leung, whose mysterious departure caused an uproar, was responsible for passports and immigration security, highly sensitive areas in the run-up to Hong Kong's transfer from Britain to China in mid-1997.
He had access to secret data on the overseas citizenships of Hong Kong officials and on mainland dissidents sheltering in Hong Kong, as well as control over immigration from China.
Leung said it was impossible for anyone in his department to leak sensitive information.

"The Immigration Department has a very secure (computer) system to prevent confidential information leaking," he said. "Any person, including the director, who has made any access, would be recorded in the system.
"There is no chance for me to cheat."
Leung told the panel he was summoned by the Secretary for the Civil Service, Lam Woon-kwong, on July 5.

"During the meeting, he said the government wanted me to resign immediately. He said if I didn't put in my resignation letter before 5 p.m. the Hong Kong government would take measures to force me out," Leung said.
"I asked him why. Mr Lam replied that was because the government did not trust me any more.
"I asked him why the government didn't trust me. He said, 'you should know'. But I still don't," Leung testified.
The Hong Kong government had earlier said Leung's early retirement, announced on July 6, was for personal reasons and had flatly refused to elaborate since.

But speaking to reporters later on Friday, secretary for civil service Lam said it was Leung who decided to retire when presented with a choice between that or waiting for Lam to make a case to Governor Chris Patten that his retirement would be desirable in the interest of the public.
"It was Mr Leung's own choice to choose to retire rather than to face Colonial Regulation 59 action," Lam told reporters.
Regulation 59 is one under which the government would make a case that a civil servant's retirement would be desirable.
Lam also refused to disclose why the government contemplated Leung's retirement and skirted questions on whether Patten had known of the matter beforehand.

"While an inquiry is going on, we have many legal considerations and we need to examine Mr Leung's testimony before we can decide whether to reveal anything further." Lam also said London was not involved in the matter.

Leung, who worked for the government for 30 years and headed the immigration department for seven years, said the ICAC launched an investigation into his affairs in October 1995. He said he was cleared the following April.
The ICAC said in a statement on Friday its investigation ended due to insufficient evidence.

The Legislative Council panel will summon Lam and his deputy to testify on January 23. Panel chairman Ip Kwok-him told reporters after the four-hour session with Leung that panel members did not rule out also asking Patten and his deputy, Anson Chan, to testify.
